opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing to say is that o1 is a genuinely different beast from the autoregressive LLMs we'd been testing before. We started calling these "large reasoning models" rather than LLMs, because whatever OpenAI is doing, likely some reinforcement learning over generated chains of thought plus significant inference-time search, it's not just next-token completion anymore. And to be fair, the improvement on PlanBench was real. On the plain Blocksworld problems, where earlier models like GPT-4 had been stuck at fairly modest accuracy, o1 did dramatically better. I don't want to be the person who moves the goalposts and pretends that didn't happen.

But the interesting part is what happens when you push on it. Take Mystery Blocksworld, where we keep the same underlying problem structure but obfuscate the action and predicate names so the model can't lean on what it has memorized about blocks and stacking. The older LLMs essentially collapsed there, close to zero. o1 does much better than that, but it's still far from robust. As you increase problem size, as plans need more steps, performance falls off quite steeply. And when we gave it unsolvable instances, it would quite often confidently hand you a "plan" anyway, or offer some rationalization for why it should work. A sound planner simply doesn't do that.

So my interpretation is this: o1 has moved from pure approximate retrieval toward something that does a bit more actual search at inference time, and that helps. But it still gives no guarantees. You can't tell when it's right, and it isn't cheap. You're paying per reasoning token, and those hidden tokens add up, sometimes by orders of magnitude compared to a standard LLM call. Meanwhile, a classical planner like Fast Downward solves these problems essentially instantly, correctly, and for practically nothing.

That's why I keep coming back to the LLM-Modulo idea. If you care about correctness, you pair these models with external verifiers, and then even a cheaper LLM in a generate-and-test loop can match or beat o1 at a fraction of the cost, with guarantees. So o1 is real progress, I'll grant that. But "it reasons" should be a claim we test, not one we take on faith because the output reads like reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first let me say that O1 is a genuinely different kind of system from the LLMs we had been testing before. When we ran the earlier models, GPT-4, Claude, Llama and so on, on Blocksworld, they were all stuck somewhere around 50 to 60 percent accuracy on the plain problems, and on the obfuscated Mystery Blocksworld version they were essentially at zero. O1 preview jumped to something like 97 percent on plain Blocksworld, and on Mystery Blocksworld it went from zero to somewhere around 50 percent. So I don't want to be dismissive of that. That is a real quantitative jump, and it tells me OpenAI is doing something at inference time, some kind of reinforcement learning over chains of thought, that goes beyond autoregressive token prediction. I have been calling these things LRMs, large reasoning models, rather than LLMs, precisely because I think they deserve a separate category.

But then there are several caveats. The first is that the performance degrades quite quickly as the plan length grows. Once you get to problems that need 20, 30, 40 step plans, accuracy falls off a cliff, which is exactly what you would expect from an approximate retrieval and search process rather than a sound planning procedure. The second, and to me more important, is the unsolvable instances. When we gave O1 problems that have no solution, it would very confidently produce a plan a good fraction of the time. A real planner tells you the problem is unsolvable. O1 is not doing that reliably, so it still doesn't know what it doesn't know, and that matters enormously for any safety-critical use.

Third, the cost. O1 consumes an enormous number of reasoning tokens, and you are paying for them, and you cannot even see them. Fast Downward solves these same instances in milliseconds for essentially zero cost with a guarantee of correctness. So from an engineering standpoint, if you have a planning problem, you would still be a bit crazy to send it to O1 rather than a planner.

And finally, because we don't know what is going on inside, we really cannot characterize it the way we can characterize a search algorithm. We don't know if it is doing something like learned search, or whether it has absorbed solutions from the enormous amount of PlanBench-style data that is now on the web. So my interpretation is that it is an impressive step, it has made me update, but it is still an approximate reasoner. The right way to use these things remains what we have been calling LLM-Modulo, where you put a verifier or a sound planner in the loop rather than trusting the model's output on its own.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish doing better on a planning benchmark from being a reliable planner. O1’s performance is encouraging in the first sense: giving the system more computation at inference time appears to help. But that doesn’t, by itself, tell us what mechanism is producing the improvement, or establish that the system can reliably solve arbitrary planning problems.

In PlanBench, the question is not whether a plan sounds reasonable. You have an initial state, actions with preconditions and effects, and a goal. You can check whether each action is executable and whether the resulting state satisfies the goal. That external check matters much more than how convincing the accompanying explanation is.

I would also want to look at how performance changes as problems become harder, and whether it survives changes to the names and presentation that leave the underlying planning problem intact. Those comparisons help distinguish robust planning ability from success that depends on familiar patterns.

So I take improvement seriously, but I wouldn’t jump from improvement to ‘planning is solved.’ The practical opportunity is to use these models to propose candidate plans and combine them with a verifier that can actually establish whether those plans work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an interesting improvement, but we should be careful about what we infer from it. PlanBench asks whether a system can produce a sequence of actions that actually achieves a goal while respecting the rules of the domain. A plausible-looking plan isn’t enough; we can check whether it works.

O1 does substantially better on some of these problems than earlier models. That deserves to be acknowledged. But success on familiar planning domains doesn’t by itself establish a general planning capability. One of the things we look at is what happens when you change the names of actions and objects while preserving the underlying planning problem. If performance drops substantially, then the system’s success is sensitive to the presentation, even though the formal reasoning required is unchanged.

So my interpretation is that additional inference-time computation can help, but we shouldn’t equate that with having a reliable planner. The useful question is whether the improvement survives changes in representation and increasing problem difficulty. And for applications where correctness matters, I would still want an external verifier checking the resulting plan.
